title: The Clay Boat Rescue
summary_zh: 一团会沉的材料，改变形状后能否浮起来？
story:
The science club has a small tub of water and a lump of modeling clay. Leo rolls the clay into a ball and drops it in. It sinks.

Pip announces a rescue mission for the clay submarine.

Maya takes the clay out and dries it. What if we change its shape without adding or removing any clay?

She makes a wide little bowl with raised sides. When she places it carefully on the water, it floats.

The material is the same, Leo says. So why is the result different?

Ms. Park asks them to notice how much space the bowl shape takes up. Water pushes upward on objects. A floating boat displaces enough water for that upward push to balance its weight.

The hollow shape keeps water out while allowing the boat to push aside more water before it is submerged.

Leo puts a small block into the boat. It sits lower. He adds more, one at a time. Eventually, water comes over the edge and the boat sinks.

Pip writes a passenger rule: Do not invite the entire classroom.

They make a second boat with higher sides and compare the designs. They record their results instead of assuming that every wider or taller boat will always be better.

At the end, Pip thanks the rescue team.

The submarine has returned to boat life, he says. It has requested a smaller guest list.
fact: Water exerts an upward force called buoyancy. An object floating at rest displaces water whose weight matches its own. A boat's overall shape, including the space that keeps water out, matters. A material that sinks as a solid lump can be part of a floating hollow boat.
recap: The same clay sank as a ball and floated as a hollow boat. Adding blocks made the boat sit lower until water came over the edge. The experiment connected shape, displaced water, and carrying capacity.
phrases: It is made of the same material.
What happens if we change the shape?
It sits lower in the water.
question: Did Maya need a different material to make the clay float?
answer: No. She changed the shape into a hollow boat that could displace enough water while keeping water out.
wonder: What features would you try in a model boat that has to carry a few small blocks?

title: The Plant by the Window
summary_zh: 植物不会吃三明治，却有自己的制造食物方式。
story:
Maya notices a plant leaning toward the classroom window. Leo turns its pot to make the desk look tidier.

Several days later, the new growth is bending toward the light again.

It likes the view, Leo says.

Pip offers the plant a picture of mountains. The plant does not respond.

Ms. Park explains that light matters for more than a nice view. Green plants use light energy to make sugars from water and carbon dioxide.

Is that the plant's lunch? Maya asks.

Sugars provide material and energy for life, says Ms. Park. The process is called photosynthesis.

Leo looks at the soil. Then the soil is not simply a bowl of food that the plant eats?

Soil provides support, water, and minerals, but the plant makes sugars using light, Ms. Park explains.

The club starts an observation notebook. They record the date, where the pot stands, and what the leaves look like. They continue normal care instead of changing everything at once.

Pip draws a restaurant menu for the plant: light, water, and air, with a sensible supply of minerals.

No sandwiches? Leo asks.

Not for this customer, says Maya.

One morning, a new leaf opens. The club celebrates quietly.

Pip asks whether the plant would like a loyalty card.

It already comes to this window every day, Leo says. I think it is a regular customer.
fact: Green plants use photosynthesis to make sugars from water and carbon dioxide using light energy. Oxygen is released in the process. Roots take up water and minerals, while leaves exchange gases with the air. Some growing plant parts bend toward light, a response called phototropism.
recap: The plant's growth turned toward the window. The club learned why light is important and how plants make sugars. Their notebook followed changes over time while they kept caring for the plant.
phrases: What does the plant need?
It is growing toward the light.
Let us record what we notice.
question: Does a green plant get all its food simply by eating soil?
answer: No. It makes sugars through photosynthesis, using light, water, and carbon dioxide, while soil can provide water and minerals.
wonder: What differences can you notice between two leaves on the same plant?

title: The Tiny Bakers in the Dough
summary_zh: 面团慢慢鼓起来，是谁在里面工作？
story:
The club visits a bakery before opening time. The baker shows them a bowl of dough and marks its starting height.

We will check it again later, she says.

Pip stares at the bowl. I am ready to watch every millimeter.

While they wait, the baker shows them ingredients. One is yeast, a living organism so small that an individual cell needs magnification to be seen clearly.

Leo looks closely at the packet. Are there tiny workers with tiny hats?

No hats, the baker says. But yeast does useful work. It uses sugars and releases carbon dioxide gas. The dough traps many gas bubbles and expands.

When they return, the dough has risen above the original mark.

It has grown without anyone adding more flour, Maya says.

The baker explains that the trapped gas has increased its volume. She does not say that a larger dough ball must contain more flour.

Later, she handles the hot oven while the children watch from the visitor area. The smell of baking bread fills the room.

Pip creates a staff list: one baker, many yeast cells, and three extremely interested visitors.

Leo asks whether all tiny living things are bad.

No, says the baker. Microorganisms have many different roles. Some help us make familiar foods.

Maya writes the day's headline: Small helpers, big bubbles.

Leo adds: Excellent smell. Further taste research requested.
fact: Baker's yeast is a microscopic fungus. It can use sugars and release carbon dioxide through fermentation. Gas bubbles become trapped in dough, helping it rise. The dough's volume increases without a matching increase in the amount of flour. Baking later changes and sets the bread's structure.
recap: Yeast helped the dough expand by producing gas. The height mark made the change easy to see. The club learned that some microorganisms play useful roles in making food.
phrases: How much has it grown?
Let us compare it with the first mark.
Tiny things can make a big difference.
question: What made the dough expand while it rested?
answer: Carbon dioxide produced by yeast became trapped as gas bubbles in the dough.
wonder: What other useful things might be happening around you on a scale too small to see directly?

title: The Ice Cube's Hidden Side
summary_zh: 冰块为什么浮着，而且大部分藏在水面下面？
story:
Leo drops an ice cube into a clear cup of water. Part of it sticks out, but most of it is below the surface.

It is a very small iceberg, Maya says.

Pip draws a tiny ship on paper and holds it beside the cup. The captain reports a much bigger object underwater.

Why does the ice float? Leo asks. It is solid, so I thought it would sink.

Ms. Park explains that being solid is not enough to decide whether something floats. Ordinary ice is less dense than liquid water. For the same volume, it has less mass.

They use the idea of two equal-sized boxes. If one contains more mass packed into that space, it has greater density. The boxes are only a comparison; water molecules are not little toys in boxes.

Maya notices that the cube keeps turning slowly. She draws the visible part above the line and the larger part below it.

A photograph showing only the top could be misleading, she says.

Leo thinks of seeing only one page of a mystery story. You might miss most of the evidence.

Pip gives the paper ship a new instruction: Respect what you cannot see.

As the ice melts, the club watches its shape change.

Our iceberg is getting smaller, says Maya.

Pip folds up the ship. The captain will now explore a much drier place: the bookshelf.
fact: Ordinary ice floats in liquid water because it is less dense. Water expands when it freezes under familiar everyday conditions. Most of a floating ice cube or iceberg stays below the surface. Density compares mass with volume; size alone does not tell you how dense something is.
recap: Most of the ice cube was underwater. The club connected floating ice with lower density and learned that the visible top does not show the full size of an object.
phrases: Most of it is below the surface.
We can only see part of it.
Size alone does not tell us everything.
question: Why can ordinary ice float in liquid water?
answer: It is less dense than the surrounding liquid water.
wonder: What other situations show you only a small part of the whole picture?

title: Lights in the Deep Ocean
summary_zh: 深海里的光不需要插座，生物自己就有发光办法。
story:
The museum has a simulated deep-ocean ride. Maya, Leo, and Pip sit in a pretend research submarine. The screen outside their window grows darker as the imaginary vehicle descends.

Then a small blue light appears.

Someone forgot to turn off a lamp, Leo says.

A narrator explains that many ocean organisms can produce light through chemical reactions. The process is called bioluminescence.

Pip is impressed. Where do they plug in their chargers?

They do not need electrical sockets like you, Maya says.

The screen shows different examples. A fish has a glowing lure near its mouth. Another animal produces flashes that may confuse an attacker. Some animals use light to help them blend with faint light from above.

So light can do different jobs, Leo says. It is not just decoration.

The ride pauses at a question: Does every glowing creature make light in exactly the same way?

Maya chooses no. The narrator explains that some animals make light themselves, while others receive help from glowing bacteria.

Pip designs a submarine with a large illuminated sign: Friendly visitors. No snacks for sale.

That would make us easy to notice, Leo says.

Then I will add an off switch, replies Pip.

When they leave the exhibit, daylight fills the museum hall. Maya looks back at the dark screen.

A place can be dark, she says, and still contain many kinds of light.
fact: Bioluminescence is light produced by chemical reactions in living systems. Marine organisms use it in different ways, such as attracting prey, communicating, or defense. Some animals depend on light-producing bacteria. The glowing lure of an animal is not an electric bulb, even if it looks like a tiny lamp.
recap: The pretend submarine introduced living lights in the ocean. Different organisms used light for different purposes, and some had bacterial partners. The children separated a useful lamp comparison from the actual biology.
phrases: What is making that light?
Some use it to find food.
Others use it for protection.
question: Does a glowing ocean animal need a battery-powered light bulb?
answer: No. Bioluminescence involves chemical reactions, sometimes with help from bacteria.
wonder: If you could send one message with a pattern of lights, what would the pattern mean?

title: The Mountain with a Secret Door
summary_zh: 从火山剖面模型理解岩浆、熔岩与地球变化。
story:
At a science center, Leo sees a model volcano cut in half. Tubes and colored sections show what may lie beneath the surface.

It has secret passages, he says. Is this where a dragon lives?

Pip searches the label. No dragon residence is listed.

The educator explains that molten rock below Earth's surface is called magma. When it erupts onto the surface, it is called lava.

Same journey, different location, Maya says, writing the two names beside a drawing.

The educator shows photographs of different volcanoes. Some are broad with gentle slopes. Others are steeper. Eruptions can also look very different.

So our one model is not a picture of every volcano, Leo says.

Correct. Models help us understand selected features, but real systems vary.

They look at a map of Earth's moving plates. Many volcanoes occur near plate boundaries, but some form away from those boundaries at hot spots.

Pip wants to put a doorbell on the model. It could warn the mountain that visitors have arrived.

Scientists use instruments and observations instead, says the educator. They study signals such as small earthquakes, changes in shape, and gases.

Maya names their drawing The Mountain with a Secret Door, then adds a clear subtitle: An imaginary title for a real geological process.

Leo draws the dragon in a separate corner labeled Fiction.

Pip approves. The dragon finally has a correct address.
fact: Magma is molten rock beneath Earth's surface; lava is molten rock after it reaches the surface. Many volcanoes occur at tectonic plate boundaries, and others occur at hot spots. Scientists monitor several kinds of evidence to study volcanic activity. Volcanoes do not all have the same shape or eruption style.
recap: A cutaway model helped explain the path from underground magma to surface lava. The club compared different volcanoes and learned that one simple model cannot represent every detail.
phrases: What is happening below the surface?
It has a different name here.
This model shows only part of the story.
question: What do we call magma after it reaches the surface?
wonder: If you could see a cutaway view of one ordinary object, which object would you choose?

title: The River That Wrote in Rock
summary_zh: 大峡谷如何记录漫长变化？一个沙盘模型带来线索。
story:
Maya finds a photograph of the Grand Canyon. Bands of rock stretch across enormous walls, and a river lies far below.

Who dug that? Leo asks. They would need a very large shovel.

Pip calculates how many toy shovels the club owns. The number is not promising.

Ms. Park explains that the Colorado River and other processes shaped the canyon over a very long time. Flowing water carries material away. Weathering breaks rock down, and side streams and falling rock also help change the landscape.

The club builds a small sand tray. With their teacher, they pour a gentle stream of water over one area. A channel begins to form, and sand moves toward the lower end.

This happened quickly, Leo says. Did the real canyon form that quickly, too?

No. Our tray shows an idea about moving water and material. Its scale, materials, and time are very different from the real canyon.

Maya draws arrows showing where the sand traveled. Pip adds a sign beside the new channel: Landscape under construction.

Later, they look again at the photograph. The rock layers remind Maya of pages in a very old book.

Can we read all of it? she asks.

Scientists are still studying its history, says Ms. Park.

Leo puts away the toy shovel. He decides that patient questions are more useful than enormous digging plans.
fact: The Grand Canyon records a long history of rock formation and landscape change. The Colorado River cut downward while weathering, tributary streams, and other processes helped widen and shape the canyon. A classroom erosion model can illustrate one process without reproducing the real landscape's full history or timescale.
recap: The photograph led the club to study erosion. Water moved sand in their tray, but the tray was only a simplified model. The real canyon was shaped by several processes over a much longer time.
phrases: It changed over a long time.
Where did the material go?
Our model is much smaller.
question: Did the fast change in the sand tray prove that the Grand Canyon formed equally fast?
answer: No. The model used different materials, scale, and conditions. It illustrated a process, not the real canyon's full timescale.
wonder: Where can you notice small signs of water moving soil or sand after rain?

title: A Desert with No Sandcastle
summary_zh: 沙漠一定又热又有沙吗？南极带来一个意外答案。
story:
The geography club is playing Guess the Place. Maya reads the first clue: It is a desert.

Leo draws a hot Sun and a camel. Pip adds a sandcastle with a robot flag.

Second clue, says Maya. This place can be extremely cold.

Leo puts a scarf on the camel.

Third clue: Much of the land is covered by a thick ice sheet.

Pip looks at his sandcastle. My building material may be wrong.

The answer is Antarctica, Maya announces.

Leo is surprised. How can a place with so much ice be a desert?

Ms. Park explains that desert conditions are about very low precipitation, not simply heat or sand. Much of Antarctica receives little new snowfall. Ice can accumulate and remain over a very long time.

So the amount already stored and the amount arriving each year are different questions, Maya says.

They imagine a jar holding many old coins. Even if only a few new coins arrive each year, the jar may still contain a lot.

Pip labels the comparison carefully: Ice is not money. Please do not pay for lunch with a snowball.

Leo changes his first drawing. The camel stays on a separate page about a hot desert. Antarctica gets its own icy landscape.

The club's final clue is for every geography question: Check the definition before trusting the first picture in your head.
fact: Deserts are characterized by very low precipitation. They can be hot or cold, and they do not all consist of sand dunes. Much of Antarctica is a cold desert. Its large store of ice does not mean that it receives a large amount of new precipitation each year.
recap: Leo first imagined a hot sandy desert, but Antarctica challenged that picture. The club used the meaning of desert and distinguished stored ice from newly falling precipitation.
phrases: It is not always hot.
What does the word really mean?
Those are two different questions.
question: Must every desert be hot and sandy?
answer: No. Very low precipitation is the important feature, and deserts can be cold.
wonder: What word makes you picture one familiar example even though other examples are very different?
